system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old woman with a history of mast cell degranulation syndrome, achalasia, and coronary artery disease s/p CABG was admitted for respiratory distress and chest pain identical to prior mast cell crises. She developed symptoms during a GI clinic visit and was transferred from the ED after treatment with IV Benadryl, Solumedrol, and Dilaudid. That night, she experienced stridor and upper airway obstruction, requiring IV epinephrine and transfer to the MICU. Her symptoms resolved with her allergist’s protocol. Workup showed no cardiac ischemia, stable atelectasis on CXR, and a negative urine culture. Pain was managed with transition back to oral methadone and gabapentin. She improved over three days and was discharged home with instructions to follow up with her allergist, ENT, and psychiatrist, continue ciprofloxacin at a reduced dose, and resume all chronic medications.
problems: Mast cell neoplasms of uncertain behavior
Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified

FINDINGS: 

AP portable upright view of the chest.   Right chest wall Port-A-Cath again
noted with catheter tip extending to the upper SVC region.  Midline sternotomy
wires are again noted.  There is a calcified ovoid structure projecting over
the mediastinum likely a calcified lymph node.  There is mild basilar
atelectasis noted bilaterally.  No focal consolidation concerning for
pneumonia.  No large effusion or pneumothorax is seen.  Cardiomediastinal
silhouette is stable.  Bony structures are intact.

IMPRESSION: 

Bibasilar atelectasis.  No convincing evidence for pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you had an endoscopy today and started having trouble breathing afterward. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, right after the procedure, I suddenly felt tightness in my chest, couldn’t catch my breath, and started wheezing. I also had that familiar itching all over. It felt just like my past mast cell reactions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The anesthesia team told us they gave you your usual medications—Benadryl, Solumedrol, albuterol, and oxygen—and you responded well. You were stable during transport here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad I didn’t need intubation. It was scary, but I knew the meds would help eventually. Is this going to happen every time I have a procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a concern we share. Even though you got premedication to prevent mast cell activation, it still triggered a reaction. We’ll need to talk with your allergist about adjusting your protocol for future procedures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. My achalasia keeps getting worse, so I might need more Botox or dilation. I can’t keep going through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring you closely. Your oxygen levels are stable now, and your breathing has improved. We’ll keep you on supplemental oxygen for a few hours and watch your respiratory rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve also been feeling a bit lightheaded. Is that from the meds or the reaction?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be from the Dilaudid or the stress on your system. Your blood pressure is a little low but not concerning. We’ll keep an eye on it and make sure you’re hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just got your chest X-ray. It shows mild atelectasis at the bases—some collapse of the small airways—but no pneumonia or fluid. That’s common after sedation and explains some of the breathing trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart or lungs failing again? I’ve been worried since my last hospitalization.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, your heart looks stable. No signs of heart failure worsening or ischemia. Your ECG was normal, and your cardiac enzymes are negative. This was primarily a mast cell activation episode.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been doing well for the past few hours. Your breathing is easier, and you’re off oxygen now. We’ll keep monitoring you overnight and plan to discharge you tomorrow if you stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Should I still take my regular meds when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, resume all your chronic medications—especially for thyroid, blood pressure, and pain. Continue the inhaler as needed. And avoid NSAIDs or morphine—your allergy list shows those can trigger reactions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve made great progress. We’re clearing you to go home today. I’ll give you a note for your allergist and GI doctor to coordinate safer premedication for future procedures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up with them. Should I go to the ER if this happens again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. Use your emergency meds first—Benadryl and epinephrine if available—and go to the ER. Call your allergist right after. We want to prevent another hospitalization.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll keep my action plan handy. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy for the next few days, stay hydrated, and don’t hesitate to call your doctors if you feel off.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old woman with a history of mast cell degranulation syndrome, achalasia, and coronary artery disease s/p CABG was admitted after developing acute dyspnea, chest tightness, wheezing, and itching following an EGD with Botox injection. Despite premedication, she experienced a mast cell activation episode and was transferred from the procedure site to the ED. She responded well to her standard treatment protocol with Benadryl, Solumedrol, albuterol, and oxygen. Chest imaging showed mild bibasilar atelectasis but no pneumonia or cardiac ischemia. Her symptoms resolved, and she remained stable overnight. She was discharged the following morning with instructions to resume chronic medications, follow up with her allergist and GI specialist, and use emergency measures if future reactions occur.
